This script cleans and analyzes the Original Social Discounting Task (Long Form) data and Social Discounting Task Short-Form exported. Data can be collected using the provided Qualtrics templates or the Shiny App code, both of which save the data and variable names in a compatible format to be analyses with this script. Further explanation of the data preparation, cleaning, and analysis steps are explains in the accompanying manual. 

# Set up
This section loads all packages required for data cleaning, reshaping, and modeling.

```{r setup-options, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE
)

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(nlme)      # Hyperbolic model
library(papaja)    # APA-style plots
library(ggplot2)
library(pracma)    # For AUC calculation (trapz)
library(purrr)

rm(list=ls())

```


# User Inputs
It assumes data were exported from Qualtrics as a CSV file using **Export values** (not Export labels).

Modify your paths and filenames for your dataset. \ 

- path: folder containing the Qualtrics CSV files  
- sd_long: filename for the long-form task data  
- sd_short: filename for the short-form task data
```{r user-input, include = FALSE, message = FALSE}
# Path to folder containing the Qualtrics export
path <- "/Users/Documents/Social-Discounting-Manual/"

# Long form data file name
sd_long  <- "SDlongform_exampledata.csv"

# Short form data file name
sd_short <- "SDshortform_exampledata.csv"
```

# Model Fitting Functions
Nonlinear mixed-effects models (`nlme`) are estimated iteratively, starting from initial guesses ("starting values") for each parameter. If the starting values are far from the final estimates, the model can fail to converge or settle on a poorer solution. Rather than trying different starting values by hand, the functions below automate this step and the model comparison step. They are used for every model in this script.

**Control settings (`ctl`)** \ 

All `nlme` models use the same control settings, which allow more iterations than the defaults before the model stops.

**`fit_best_start()`** \ 

This function:

- fits the model once for every combination of starting values in a grid
- skips any combination where the model fails to converge
- keeps the converged model with the highest log-likelihood (the best-fitting solution)
- prints how many of the starting values converged

Arguments:

- `fit_fun`: a function that takes a vector of starting values and returns an `nlme` model
- `start_grid`: a data frame of starting values to try, with one column per parameter (e.g., v0 and logk), created with `expand.grid()`
- `n_extra`: the number of predictors in the model (Model 2 only). The starting values for the predictor slopes are set to 0.

A table of every starting value tried, and the estimates it reached, is saved with the model. You can view it with `attr(model, "start_search")`:

- If the converged fits reach the same log-likelihood and the same estimates, the solution is stable and does not depend on the starting values.
- If they reach different estimates with similar log-likelihoods, the model may be poorly identified and should be simplified.
- If only a few starting values converge, interpret the results with caution. If none converge, widen `start_grid` or simplify the model.

**`aic_table()`** \ 

This function takes a named list of models and returns a model comparison table (see the Model Comparison sections below). It gives the same values as `aictab()` from the AICcmodavg package, but it also works when `nlme` models are compared with the `lme` linear model, which `aictab()` does not allow.

```{r model-functions}
# Control settings used for all nlme models
ctl <- nlmeControl(msMaxIter = 1000, maxIter = 500, pnlsMaxIter = 50)

# Try a grid of starting values and keep the best-fitting model that converges
fit_best_start <- function(fit_fun, start_grid, n_extra = 0) {
  p <- ncol(start_grid)

  results <- purrr::map(seq_len(nrow(start_grid)), function(i) {
    st  <- c(unlist(start_grid[i, ]), rep(0, n_extra))
    fit <- tryCatch(fit_fun(st), error = function(e) NULL)  # failed fits return NULL
    list(start = st, fit = fit)
  })

  ok <- purrr::keep(results, ~ !is.null(.x$fit))
  if (length(ok) == 0) stop("No starting values converged. Widen start_grid or simplify the model.")

  search <- purrr::map_dfr(ok, function(r) data.frame(
    as.list(setNames(r$start[1:p], paste0("start_", names(start_grid)))),
    logLik = as.numeric(logLik(r$fit)),
    as.list(setNames(fixef(r$fit)[1:p], paste0("est_", names(start_grid)))),
    check.names = FALSE))

  best <- ok[[which.max(search$logLik)]]
  message(length(ok), " of ", nrow(start_grid), " starting values converged.")
  attr(best$fit, "start_search") <- search
  best$fit
}

# Model comparison table: K, log-likelihood, AICc, delta AICc, AICc weights
aic_table <- function(models) {
  tab <- data.frame(
    Model = names(models),
    K     = sapply(models, function(m) attr(logLik(m), "df")),  # number of parameters
    LL    = sapply(models, function(m) as.numeric(logLik(m))),  # log-likelihood
    n     = sapply(models, nobs)                                # number of observations
  )
  tab$AICc   <- -2 * tab$LL + 2 * tab$K + (2 * tab$K * (tab$K + 1)) / (tab$n - tab$K - 1)
  tab$Delta  <- tab$AICc - min(tab$AICc)
  tab$Weight <- exp(-0.5 * tab$Delta) / sum(exp(-0.5 * tab$Delta))
  tab <- tab[order(tab$AICc), ]
  tab$Cum_Weight <- cumsum(tab$Weight)
  rownames(tab) <- NULL
  tab
}
```

# SD LONG FORM
This is the data cleaning and analysis pipeline for the original Social Discounting Task

## Import Data
This section imports the Qualtrics data file and cleans the data so the SD columns and subnum columns are numeric. It also drops the first 2 header rows seen in a qualtrics output
```{r SDL import-data}
data_wide <- read.delim(
  file = paste0(path, sd_long),
  sep = ",",
  quote = "\"",
  header = TRUE
)

sd_cols <- grep("^sd\\d+_\\d$", names(data_wide), value = TRUE)

data_wide <- data_wide %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(sd_cols), ~ suppressWarnings(as.numeric(.x)))) %>%
  filter(if_any(all_of(sd_cols), ~ !is.na(.x))) %>%   # drops the 2 Qualtrics header rows
  mutate(subnum = type.convert(na_if(trimws(as.character(subnum)), ""), as.is = TRUE))  # numeric IDs stay numeric (done after the header rows are removed)

```



## Expected csv variable names
This analysis script assumes that the csv export contains the following variables.

**Subject identifier** \ 

- subnum: unique participant ID (participants without a value in subnum will be removed during data cleaning)
 

**Social Discounting Trial name structure** \ 

Each trial is named using the following structure: sd[distance]_[trial] \ 

Here is a complete list of required variables \ 

- sd1_1 – sd1_9
- sd2_1 – sd2_9
- sd5_1 – sd5_9
- sd10_1 – sd10_9
- sd20_1 – sd20_9
- sd50_1 – sd50_9
- sd100_1 – sd100_9

**Response coding** \ 

Responses should be exported from Qualtrics using Export values. \ 
For trials 1-8, expected coding is: \ 

- 0 = kept money \ 
- Positive value (80-10) = shared money (amount offered to keep - $75)

On trial 9 (keep 75 or split 75/75), the expected coding is: \ 

- -5 = kept money 
- 0 = shared money

Check to make sure your data has all of the needed column/column names
```{r SDL colnames}
names(data_wide)
```

## Data Cleaning
The following steps convert the raw Qualtrics export into participant-level indifference points that can be used for modeling.

### Reshape Data 
This removes rows that do not contain a participant ID.
The Social Discounting task contains multiple trials per distance level.  
This step converts the dataset from **wide format to long format**, which allows trial-level processing. After this step:

- `trial` contains the trial name (e.g., sd1_1, sd10_5)
- `choice` contains the participant’s response.
```{r SDL reshape_long}
data_wide2 <- data_wide[!is.na(data_wide$subnum), ]

longer_numeric <- pivot_longer(
  data_wide2,
  cols = c(
    "sd1_1","sd1_2","sd1_3","sd1_4","sd1_5","sd1_6","sd1_7","sd1_8","sd1_9",
    "sd2_1","sd2_2","sd2_3","sd2_4","sd2_5","sd2_6","sd2_7","sd2_8","sd2_9",
    "sd5_1","sd5_2","sd5_3","sd5_4","sd5_5","sd5_6","sd5_7","sd5_8","sd5_9",
    "sd10_1","sd10_2","sd10_3","sd10_4","sd10_5","sd10_6","sd10_7","sd10_8","sd10_9",
    "sd20_1","sd20_2","sd20_3","sd20_4","sd20_5","sd20_6","sd20_7","sd20_8","sd20_9",
    "sd50_1","sd50_2","sd50_3","sd50_4","sd50_5","sd50_6","sd50_7","sd50_8","sd50_9",
    "sd100_1","sd100_2","sd100_3","sd100_4","sd100_5","sd100_6","sd100_7","sd100_8","sd100_9"
  ),
  names_to = "trial",
  values_to = "choice"
)
```

### Split Trial Information
Each trial name contains two pieces of information:

- social distance (e.g., sd100)
- trial number (e.g., 9)

This step separates these into two columns:

- `distance` 
- `amount1`

REFERENCE FOR AMOUNTS: This table shows the amount offered for the participant to keep.  
The alternative option is always a $75 / $75 split. \ 

- 1 - 155
- 2 - 145
- 3 - 135
- 4 - 125
- 5 - 115
- 6 - 105
- 7 - 95
- 8 - 85
- 9 - 75
```{r SDL split-trial-info}
split_data <- separate(
  longer_numeric,
  trial,
  into = c("distance", "amount1"),
  sep = "_"
)

```

### Quality Check
This step flags participants with missing or inconsistent responses at each social distance. Each response is recoded as 0 = kept or 1 = shared (on trial 9, −5 = kept and 0 = shared). For each participant and distance, we then count:

- n_trials: the number of valid responses (should be 9)
- n_switches: the number of times the participant changes between keeping and sharing. 0 = always kept or always shared, 1 = expected pattern, 2 or more = inconsistent.

The output lists any participant × distance with fewer than 9 valid trials or more than one switch. If nothing is listed, the data are complete and consistent. Inspect any flagged rows before continuing. You can keep them, exclude them, or use the logistic regression alternative below. Report the number flagged in your Methods.
```{r SDL quality-check}
qc <- split_data %>%
  mutate(amount1 = as.numeric(amount1),
         choice  = as.numeric(choice),
         share = case_when(amount1 == 9 & choice %in% c(-5, 5) ~ 0,  # kept on trial 9
                           amount1 == 9 & choice == 0          ~ 1,  # shared on trial 9
                           amount1 != 9 & choice == 0          ~ 0,  # kept on trials 1-8
                           amount1 != 9 & choice > 0           ~ 1)) %>% # shared on trials 1-8
  arrange(subnum, distance, amount1) %>%
  group_by(subnum, distance) %>%
  summarise(n_trials   = sum(!is.na(share)),
            n_switches = sum(diff(share[!is.na(share)]) != 0),
            .groups = "drop")

qc %>% filter(n_trials < 9 | n_switches > 1)
```

### Recode Choice Values
Due to how the task is coded in Qualtrics:

For most trials: \ 

- 0 = participant kept the money

On the final trial: \ 

- -5 = participant kept the money
- 0 = participant shared

To correctly identify the crossover point, we temporarily convert:

-5 → 5

This ensures that if a participant keeps money on all trials, the final trial is selected as their maximum amount willing to forgo (we select the most positive number). \ 

Later, this value is converted back to -5 to distinguish participants who kept money on all trials whose maximum amount willing to forgo will be 0.

```{r SDL recode-choice}
split_data$choice <- ifelse(split_data$choice == -5, 5, split_data$choice)
```



### Remove Invalid/Missing Responses
This step:

- removes missing responses
- ensures `choice` values are numeric

Then we select rows where choice is above or equal to 0 (why we changed -5 to 5) to highlight valid responses
```{r SDL filter-valid-trials}
filtered_data <- split_data[!is.na(as.numeric(split_data$choice)), ]
filtered_data <- subset(filtered_data, choice == 0 | choice > 0)

```

### Convert Social Distance to Numeric
The distance labels (sd1, sd2, etc.) are converted to numeric values (1, 2, etc), creating a new column called "Distance"
```{r SDL recode-distance}
max_ratings1 <- filtered_data %>%
  dplyr::select(-any_of("X")) %>% 
  mutate(
    Distance = case_when(
      distance == "sd1" ~ 1,
      distance == "sd2" ~ 2,
      distance == "sd5" ~ 5,
      distance == "sd10" ~ 10,
      distance == "sd20" ~ 20,
      distance == "sd50" ~ 50,
      distance == "sd100" ~ 100,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    )
  )

```
### Compute Indifference Points
We calculate the **maximum amount participants were willing to forgo** for each social distance by identifying the crossover point where participants switch from keeping money to sharing (indifference point). 

First, we group decisions by Distance and select the **maximum choice value** at each social distance (the most positive number). This selects the **first** time the participant crosses over from keep to share. This maximum rating/willing to forgo is put in a new column called max_rating. Then we left_join all of the other predictor variables (if you have any other covariates)

Then, in the max_rating column, we convert 5 (kept at the last trial) back to -5. 
```{r SDL compute-indifference}
trial_filtered_data <- max_ratings1 %>%
  group_by(subnum, Distance, distance) %>%
  summarise(max_rating = max(choice), .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(
    max_ratings1 %>%
      distinct(subnum, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
      dplyr::select(-Distance, -distance, -amount1, -choice),
    by = "subnum"
  )
trial_filtered_data$max_rating <- ifelse(trial_filtered_data$max_rating == 5, -5, trial_filtered_data$max_rating)

```

### Data Check
This table shows the distribution of indifference points across participants.

These values reflect the maximum amount participants were willing to forgo at each social distance.

Interpretation:

- 80 = shared on the first trial
- 70–10 = switched to sharing on trials 2-8 (later crossover = less generous)
- 0 = shared on the final trial
- -5 = kept money on all trials
```{r SDL data-check}
table(trial_filtered_data$max_rating)
```


## OPTIONAL: Missing Data - Data Cleaning Alternative
The standard social discounting pipeline identifies indifference points by locating the crossover trial where participants switch from keeping money to sharing. This requires complete data within each social distance. However, in some context (neuroimaging studies, online data collection without request response), participants may have a lot of missing data on individual trials and you may not want to pairwise delete. To address this, we use a trial-level logistic regression approach, which uses all available trials to model choices directly and estimate the indifference point.

### Reshape Data and Split Trial Information
```{r SDL reshape_long2, eval = FALSE}
data_wide2 <- data_wide[!is.na(data_wide$subnum), ]

longer_numeric <- pivot_longer(
  data_wide2,
  cols = c(
    "sd1_1","sd1_2","sd1_3","sd1_4","sd1_5","sd1_6","sd1_7","sd1_8","sd1_9",
    "sd2_1","sd2_2","sd2_3","sd2_4","sd2_5","sd2_6","sd2_7","sd2_8","sd2_9",
    "sd5_1","sd5_2","sd5_3","sd5_4","sd5_5","sd5_6","sd5_7","sd5_8","sd5_9",
    "sd10_1","sd10_2","sd10_3","sd10_4","sd10_5","sd10_6","sd10_7","sd10_8","sd10_9",
    "sd20_1","sd20_2","sd20_3","sd20_4","sd20_5","sd20_6","sd20_7","sd20_8","sd20_9",
    "sd50_1","sd50_2","sd50_3","sd50_4","sd50_5","sd50_6","sd50_7","sd50_8","sd50_9",
    "sd100_1","sd100_2","sd100_3","sd100_4","sd100_5","sd100_6","sd100_7","sd100_8","sd100_9"
  ),
  names_to = "trial",
  values_to = "choice"
)

split_data <- separate(
  longer_numeric,
  trial,
  into = c("distance", "amount1"),
  sep = "_"
)

```

### Recode Choice Values \ 
Here we recode the amount1 column to be amount_value which reflects the amount of money forgone when choosing to share, such that higher values correspond to greater amount forgone. We also recode the choice column to be binary where 0 is keep and 1 is share.
```{r SDL filter-valid-trials2, eval = FALSE}
split_data$choice <- as.numeric(split_data$choice)

logit_data <- split_data %>%
  mutate(
    amount1 = as.numeric(amount1),
    
    # Convert trial number to actual dollar values
    amount_value = case_when(
      amount1 == 1 ~ 80,
      amount1 == 2 ~ 70,
      amount1 == 3 ~ 60,
      amount1 == 4 ~ 50,
      amount1 == 5 ~ 40,
      amount1 == 6 ~ 30,
      amount1 == 7 ~ 20,
      amount1 == 8 ~ 10,
      amount1 == 9 ~ 0, 
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    ),
    
    Distance = case_when(
      distance == "sd1" ~ 1,
      distance == "sd2" ~ 2,
      distance == "sd5" ~ 5,
      distance == "sd10" ~ 10,
      distance == "sd20" ~ 20,
      distance == "sd50" ~ 50,
      distance == "sd100" ~ 100,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    ),
    
    # Recode choice: 0 = keep, 1 = share
    choice_binary = case_when(
      amount1 == 9 & choice == -5 ~ 0,
      amount1 == 9 & choice == 0 ~ 1,
      
      amount1 != 9 & choice == 0 ~ 0,
      amount1 != 9 & choice > 0 ~ 1
    )
  )
```

### Estimate Indifference Point \ 
Here we estimate indifference points using a trial-level logistic regression model for each participant at each social distance. This approach uses all available observed trials rather than relying on a single crossover point.

Participants with no variability in responses (i.e., always choosing to keep or always choosing to share) are assigned boundary values of the task range, as logistic regression cannot be reliably estimated in the absence of response variability. Additionally, the indifference point for participants with fewer than 3 responses for a social distance are not estimated. We model the probability of choosing to share (choice_binary = 1) as a function of the amount of money forgone (amount_value). The resulting function describes how decision probability changes as a function of increasing monetary cost. The indifference point is defined as the value of amount_value at which the participant is equally likely to keep or share the reward (i.e., P(share) = 0.5). This is computed analytically from the fitted logistic regression coefficients. 
```{r estimate-ind, eval = FALSE}
indifference_data <- logit_data %>%
  group_by(subnum, Distance) %>%
  group_modify(~{
    
    df <- .x
    
    # Remove missing rows (handled automatically, but explicit here)
    df <- df %>% filter(!is.na(choice_binary), !is.na(amount_value))
    
    # Handle edge cases
    if (nrow(df) < 3) {
      return(tibble(max_rating = NA_real_))
    }
    
    if (all(df$choice_binary == 1)) {
      return(tibble(max_rating = 80))  # always shared
    }
    
    if (all(df$choice_binary == 0)) {
      return(tibble(max_rating = 0))    # always kept
    }
    
    # Fit logistic regression
    fit <- glm(choice_binary ~ amount_value,
               family = binomial,
               data = df)
    
    coefs <- coef(fit)
    
    # Compute indifference point (P = 0.5)
    v <- -coefs[1] / coefs[2]
    
    tibble(max_rating = v)
  }) %>%
  ungroup()

trial_filtered_data <- indifference_data %>%
  left_join(
    logit_data %>%
      distinct(subnum, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
      dplyr::select(-Distance, -distance, -amount1, -amount_value, -choice_binary, -choice),
    by = "subnum"
  )

summary(trial_filtered_data$max_rating)



```


## Analysis
This code uses the cleaned data to run the hyperbolic model, extract individual logk values and calculate individual AUC values

### Hyperbolic Model
The Social Discounting Task is typically analyzed using a hyperbolic discounting model, which estimates how generosity decreases as social distance increases.

The model estimates two parameters:

- v0: baseline generosity (at social distance = 0)
- logk: social discounting rate

Higher (less negative) logk values indicate steeper discounting across social distance.

#### Model 1: Base model (no predictors)
This model estimates the hyperbolic social discounting function without including any predictors. It is used to obtain **participant-level discounting parameters**, including logk, which reflects the rate of social discounting.
In most cases, researchers should run this model first and extract the **individual logk estimates** from it. These logk values can then be used in subsequent analyses (e.g., regression models) that include covariates or group variables.
Most users should run this model.

Starting values are chosen automatically with `fit_best_start()` (see Model Fitting Functions). `start_grid` lists the starting values to try for v0 and logk. Widen it if no starting values converge.

```{r SDL base-model}
# Starting values to try (long form: v0 between 0 and 80)
start_grid <- expand.grid(v0 = c(40, 60, 80), logk = c(-6, -4, -2, -1, 0))

hyp_fit <- function(st) nlme(as.numeric(max_rating) ~ v0 / (1 + exp(logk) * Distance),
                             fixed     = list(v0 ~ 1, logk ~ 1),
                             random    = v0 + logk ~ 1 | subnum,
                             start     = st,
                             data      = trial_filtered_data,
                             control   = ctl,
                             na.action = na.omit)

base_model_long <- fit_best_start(hyp_fit, start_grid)
summary(base_model_long)
attr(base_model_long, "start_search")   # every starting value tried and the result it reached
```

##### Comparison Models
We compare the hyperbolic model with an exponential and a linear model to confirm that the hyperbolic model fits best.

- **Exponential model:** like the hyperbolic model, it is parameterized with logk (k = exp(logk)), which keeps k positive. Its starting values are found with `fit_best_start()`. Note that the exponential logk is not on the same scale as the hyperbolic logk, so the two should not be compared directly.
- **Linear model:** this model is linear, so it is fit with `lme()`, which does not need starting values. `method = "ML"` is required so that its AICc can be compared with the `nlme` models.
```{r SDL alt models base}
# Exponential model
exp_fit <- function(st) nlme(as.numeric(max_rating) ~ v0 * exp(-exp(logk) * Distance),
                             fixed     = list(v0 ~ 1, logk ~ 1),
                             random    = v0 + logk ~ 1 | subnum,
                             start     = st,
                             data      = trial_filtered_data,
                             control   = ctl,
                             na.action = na.omit)

exponential_model_base <- fit_best_start(exp_fit, start_grid)
summary(exponential_model_base)

# Linear model
linear_model_base <- lme(as.numeric(max_rating) ~ Distance,
                         random    = ~ Distance | subnum,
                         data      = trial_filtered_data,
                         method    = "ML",
                         na.action = na.omit,
                         control   = lmeControl(opt = "optim"))
summary(linear_model_base)
```

##### Model Comparison (AICc Weights)
After fitting the hyperbolic, exponential, and linear models, we compare their relative fit using Akaike's Information Criterion corrected for sample size (AICc). AICc balances model fit and complexity: lower values indicate better-fitting models, with a penalty for additional parameters.

The `aic_table()` function (see Model Fitting Functions) returns one row per model, ranked from best to worst fit:

- K: number of estimated parameters
- LL: log-likelihood
- AICc
- Delta: ΔAICc, the difference between each model's AICc and the lowest AICc among the models
- Weight: AICc weight, the relative likelihood that each model is the best of the candidate models, calculated as
$$w_i = \frac{\exp(-\Delta_i / 2)}{\sum_j \exp(-\Delta_j / 2)}$$
- Cum_Weight: cumulative weight

We also calculate AIC weights directly from each model's AIC, without the small-sample correction:

- Extracts AIC for each model using `AIC()`
- Computes ΔAIC as the difference from the lowest AIC
- Calculates AIC weights using the same formula as above

With large samples (840 observations in the example data), AIC and AICc are nearly identical, so both tables lead to the same conclusions.

Interpretation: \ 

In most cases, the hyperbolic model will have the lowest AICc, so the exponential and linear models will have positive ΔAICc values. \ 
ΔAICc < 2 → substantial support (models are essentially equivalent) \ 
ΔAICc 4–7 → considerably less support \ 
ΔAICc > 10 → essentially no support (the model with the lower AICc fits better) \ 

AICc weights sum to 1 across the models. An AICc weight of 1 for the hyperbolic model means it is overwhelmingly the best-fitting model compared to the exponential and linear alternatives.
```{r SDL AIC_base}
models_base <- list(hyperbolic  = base_model_long,
                    exponential = exponential_model_base,
                    linear      = linear_model_base)

AICc_table_base <- aic_table(models_base)
print(AICc_table_base)

# AIC weights (manual)
AICs_base <- sapply(models_base, AIC)
delta_base <- AICs_base - min(AICs_base)
weights_base <- exp(-0.5 * delta_base) / sum(exp(-0.5 * delta_base))

AIC_table_base <- data.frame(
  Model = names(AICs_base),
  AIC = as.numeric(AICs_base),
  Delta = delta_base,
  Weight = weights_base
)
print(AIC_table_base)
```
##### Extract logk
Below we extract individual logk values for each participant. 
In most cases, logk values should be extracted from the base model (Model 1). This ensures that individual discounting estimates are derived directly from task behavior and are not influenced by predictors included in the hyperbolic model. These participant-level logk values can then be used in subsequent analyses (e.g., regression models with covariates).

```{r SDL base logk}
cf <- coef(base_model_long)                   # fixed + random, one row per subnum
individual_logk_df_base <- data.frame(
  subnum    = type.convert(rownames(cf), as.is = TRUE),
  logk_base = cf$logk
)
head(individual_logk_df_base)
```

##### Check Against the True Values (Practice Data Only)
The practice data were simulated from known parameters, saved in `SDlongform_exampledata_trueparameters.csv`. This chunk compares the estimated logk with the true logk. It runs only if that file is in the `path` folder, so it is skipped for real data.

```{r SDL check true logk}
true_file_long <- file.path(path, sub("\\.csv$", "_trueparameters.csv", sd_long))

if (file.exists(true_file_long)) {
  true_long <- read.csv(true_file_long)

  check_long <- individual_logk_df_base %>%
    inner_join(true_long, by = "subnum")

  print(cor.test(check_long$logk, check_long$logk_base)) # correlation between true and estimated logk
}
```


##### Extracting AUC \ 
Area under the curve (AUC) is computed using the trapezoidal method (trapz) across the observed social distance values (1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100). Because AUC is calculated over the actual range of x-values included in the task, the total span of the social distance axis is 100 − 1 = 99 units. The maximum possible AUC therefore corresponds to a participant consistently selecting the maximum forgone amount (80) across this range, yielding a value of 99 × 80 = 7,920. Observed AUC values are divided by 7,920 to yield a normalized index bounded between 0 and 1.
```{r SDL base AUC}
trial_filtered_data2 <- dplyr::left_join(
  trial_filtered_data,
  individual_logk_df_base,
  by = "subnum"
)

AUC_long <- trial_filtered_data2 %>%
  group_by(subnum) %>%
  summarise(AUC = trapz(as.numeric(Distance), as.numeric(max_rating))/7920, .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(
    trial_filtered_data2 %>%
      dplyr::distinct(subnum, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
      dplyr::select(-max_rating, -Distance, -any_of(c("distance","amount1","choice","trial"))),
    by = "subnum"
  )

cor.test(AUC_long$logk_base, AUC_long$AUC)
mean(AUC_long$AUC)
sd(AUC_long$AUC)
range(AUC_long$AUC)

```

#### Model 2: Model With Predictors (Optional)
You may want to examine how participant characteristics predict differences in the hyperbolic discounting function itself.
This model allows predictors (e.g., demographic variables, personality traits, or group membership) to explain variability in the discounting rate (logk).
This step is **optional** and is typically used only if the goal is to test predictors **directly within the hyperbolic model**, rather than analyzing extracted logk values in a separate model.

**Tips for using this model:**

Modify the predictors in the example to match the variables available in your dataset.
Set `n_extra` in `fit_best_start()` to the number of predictors in the model (5 in this example). The starting values for the predictor slopes are set to 0.
```{r SDL hyperbolic-predictor-example, eval = FALSE}
pred_hyp_fit <- function(st) nlme(as.numeric(max_rating) ~ v0 / (1 + exp(logk) * Distance),
                                  fixed     = list(v0 ~ 1,
                                                   logk ~ as.numeric(Male) + as.numeric(age) + as.numeric(income) +
                                                          as.numeric(FIT_sum) + as.numeric(Group_var)),
                                  random    = v0 + logk ~ 1 | subnum,
                                  start     = st,
                                  data      = trial_filtered_data,
                                  control   = ctl,
                                  na.action = na.omit)

predictor_model <- fit_best_start(pred_hyp_fit, start_grid, n_extra = 5)
summary(predictor_model)
attr(predictor_model, "start_search")
```


##### Comparison Models
We compare the hyperbolic model with an exponential and a linear model to confirm that the hyperbolic model fits best.

- **Exponential model:** like the hyperbolic model, it is parameterized with logk (k = exp(logk)), which keeps k positive. Its starting values are found with `fit_best_start()`. Note that the exponential logk is not on the same scale as the hyperbolic logk, so the two should not be compared directly.
- **Linear model:** this model is linear, so it is fit with `lme()`, which does not need starting values. `method = "ML"` is required so that its AICc can be compared with the `nlme` models. In `lme()`, a predictor's effect on the slope is written as an interaction with Distance (`Distance:predictor`), so the predictors affect the rate of decline, as in the hyperbolic and exponential models.
```{r SDL alt models pred, eval = FALSE}
# Exponential model
pred_exp_fit <- function(st) nlme(as.numeric(max_rating) ~ v0 * exp(-exp(logk) * Distance),
                                  fixed     = list(v0 ~ 1,
                                                   logk ~ as.numeric(Male) + as.numeric(age) + as.numeric(income) +
                                                          as.numeric(FIT_sum) + as.numeric(Group_var)),
                                  random    = v0 + logk ~ 1 | subnum,
                                  start     = st,
                                  data      = trial_filtered_data,
                                  control   = ctl,
                                  na.action = na.omit)

exponential_model_pred <- fit_best_start(pred_exp_fit, start_grid, n_extra = 5)
summary(exponential_model_pred)

# Linear model
linear_model_pred <- lme(as.numeric(max_rating) ~ Distance +
                           Distance:(as.numeric(Male) + as.numeric(age) + as.numeric(income) +
                                     as.numeric(FIT_sum) + as.numeric(Group_var)),
                         random    = ~ Distance | subnum,
                         data      = trial_filtered_data,
                         method    = "ML",
                         na.action = na.omit,
                         control   = lmeControl(opt = "optim"))
summary(linear_model_pred)
```

##### Model Comparison (AICc Weights)
After fitting the hyperbolic, exponential, and linear models, we compare their relative fit using Akaike's Information Criterion corrected for sample size (AICc). AICc balances model fit and complexity: lower values indicate better-fitting models, with a penalty for additional parameters.

The `aic_table()` function (see Model Fitting Functions) returns one row per model, ranked from best to worst fit:

- K: number of estimated parameters
- LL: log-likelihood
- AICc
- Delta: ΔAICc, the difference between each model's AICc and the lowest AICc among the models
- Weight: AICc weight, the relative likelihood that each model is the best of the candidate models, calculated as
$$w_i = \frac{\exp(-\Delta_i / 2)}{\sum_j \exp(-\Delta_j / 2)}$$
- Cum_Weight: cumulative weight

We also calculate AIC weights directly from each model's AIC, without the small-sample correction:

- Extracts AIC for each model using `AIC()`
- Computes ΔAIC as the difference from the lowest AIC
- Calculates AIC weights using the same formula as above

With large samples (840 observations in the example data), AIC and AICc are nearly identical, so both tables lead to the same conclusions.

Interpretation: \ 

In most cases, the hyperbolic model will have the lowest AICc, so the exponential and linear models will have positive ΔAICc values. \ 
ΔAICc < 2 → substantial support (models are essentially equivalent) \ 
ΔAICc 4–7 → considerably less support \ 
ΔAICc > 10 → essentially no support (the model with the lower AICc fits better) \ 

AICc weights sum to 1 across the models. An AICc weight of 1 for the hyperbolic model means it is overwhelmingly the best-fitting model compared to the exponential and linear alternatives.
```{r SDL AIC_pred, eval = FALSE}
models_pred <- list(hyperbolic  = predictor_model,
                    exponential = exponential_model_pred,
                    linear      = linear_model_pred)

# AICc table (same values as aictab() in the AICcmodavg package)
AICc_table_pred <- aic_table(models_pred)
AICc_table_pred

# AIC weights (manual)
AICs_pred <- sapply(models_pred, AIC)
delta_pred <- AICs_pred - min(AICs_pred)
weights_pred <- exp(-0.5 * delta_pred) / sum(exp(-0.5 * delta_pred))
weights_pred

AIC_table_pred <- data.frame(
  Model = names(AICs_pred),
  AIC = as.numeric(AICs_pred),
  Delta = delta_pred,
  Weight = weights_pred
)
AIC_table_pred
```

##### Extracting logk values
In the predictor model, each participant's logk depends on their predictor values. It is calculated as the participant-specific intercept (the fixed intercept plus that participant's random effect) plus each fixed slope multiplied by the participant's value on that predictor.
The code below:

- uses coef() to get each participant's model coefficients. The logk intercept already includes the participant's random effect.
- selects one row per participant from the data and puts the rows in the same order as the model output. Participants the model excluded (e.g., because of missing covariates) are dropped.
- creates a predictor matrix with each participant's covariate values. The predictors must match those in the hyperbolic model, in the same order.
- multiplies each participant's predictor values by the corresponding coefficients and sums them to get that participant's logk
- creates a dataset (individual_logk_df_pred) with one row per participant, containing the participant ID and estimated logk.

```{r SDL pred logk, eval = FALSE}
cf  <- coef(predictor_model)
pp  <- trial_filtered_data %>% distinct(subnum, .keep_all = TRUE)
pp  <- pp[match(type.convert(rownames(cf), as.is = TRUE), pp$subnum), ] #puts the rows in the same order as the participants in cf. also drops anyone that the model left out (ex: for missing a covariate)
X <- model.matrix(~ as.numeric(Male) + as.numeric(age) + as.numeric(income) +
                    as.numeric(FIT_sum) + as.numeric(Group_var),
                  data = pp) #builds a matrix

individual_logk_df_pred <- data.frame(
  subnum    = pp$subnum,
  logk_pred = rowSums(X * as.matrix(cf[, grep("^logk", names(cf))]))
)
```


##### Extracting AUC
```{r SDL pred AUC, eval = FALSE}
if (exists("AUC_long")) {
  AUC_long <- dplyr::left_join(
    AUC_long,
    individual_logk_df_pred,
    by = "subnum"
  )
} else {
  trial_filtered_data3 <- dplyr::left_join(
    trial_filtered_data,
    individual_logk_df_pred,
    by = "subnum"
  )
  
  AUC_long <- trial_filtered_data3 %>%
    group_by(subnum) %>%
    summarise(AUC = trapz(as.numeric(Distance), as.numeric(max_rating))/7920, .groups = "drop") %>%
    left_join(
      trial_filtered_data3 %>%
        dplyr::distinct(subnum, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
        dplyr::select(-max_rating, -Distance, -any_of(c("distance","amount1","choice","trial"))),
      by = "subnum"
    )
}

```


### Graph of Social Discounting curve 
This code generates a plot of participants’ generosity across social distance, scaled as a proportion of the maximum possible amount (percentage). The workflow automatically adapts based on whether the dataset contains a grouping variable (Group):

- With "Group_var" present: The data are summarized separately for each group. The plot displays one line per group with shaded ribbons representing ±1 standard error of the mean. Groups are automatically labeled “Group1” and “Group2,” and color-coded for clarity.
- Without "Group_var": The data are summarized across all participants, producing a single hyperbolic curve with its standard error ribbon.

This approach ensures the graph works whether or not multiple groups are present, providing a clear visualization of social discounting behavior in your sample.

```{r SDL graph, echo = FALSE}
trial_filtered_data <- trial_filtered_data %>% mutate(percentage = as.numeric(max_rating) / 80)

if("Group_var" %in% colnames(trial_filtered_data)) {
  
  summary_data_l <- trial_filtered_data %>%
    group_by(Distance, Group_var) %>%
    summarise(payment = mean(percentage, na.rm = TRUE),
              ste = sd(percentage, na.rm = TRUE)/sqrt(n()),
              .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(Group = ifelse(Group_var == 1, "Group1", "Group2"))
  
  colors_mapping <- c("Group2" = "coral", "Group1" = "darkturquoise")
  
} else {
  
  summary_data_l <- trial_filtered_data %>%
    group_by(Distance) %>%
    summarise(payment = mean(percentage, na.rm = TRUE),
              ste = sd(percentage, na.rm = TRUE)/sqrt(n()),
              .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(Group = "All Participants")
  
  colors_mapping <- c("All Participants" = "darkturquoise")
}

# Plot curve
SD_APAplot_long <- ggplot(summary_data_l, aes(x = Distance, y = payment, color = Group, fill = Group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = payment - ste, ymax = payment + ste), alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(title = "Hyperbolic Social Discounting Curve",
       x = "Social Distance",
       y = "Proportion of $ Willing to Forgo") +
  scale_color_manual(values = colors_mapping) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colors_mapping) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_apa(base_size = 10, box = FALSE) +
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = "sans"),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 10, margin = margin(t = 10)),
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 10, margin = margin(r = 10)),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.line = element_line(colour = "black"),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 9)
  )

print(SD_APAplot_long)
```

# SD SHORT FORM

## Import Data

This section imports the Qualtrics data file.
```{r SDS import-data}

data_wide_short <- read.delim(
  file = paste0(path, sd_short),
  sep = ",",
  quote = "\"",
  header = TRUE
)

sd_cols <- grep("X*_SDshort_decision", names(data_wide_short), value = TRUE)

data_wide_short <- data_wide_short %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(sd_cols), ~ suppressWarnings(as.numeric(.x)))) %>%
  filter(if_any(all_of(sd_cols), ~ !is.na(.x))) %>%   # drops the 2 Qualtrics header rows
  mutate(subnum = type.convert(na_if(trimws(as.character(subnum)), ""), as.is = TRUE))  # numeric IDs stay numeric (done after the header rows are removed)


```


- 1_SDshort_decision = N1
- 2_SDshort_decision = N2
- 3_SDshort_decision = N5
- 4_SDshort_decision = N10
- 5_SDshort_decision = N20
- 6_SDshort_decision = N50
- 7_SDshort_decision = N100

## Data Cleaning
The following steps convert the raw Qualtrics export into participant-level indifference points that can be used for modeling.

### Reshape Data 
This removes rows that do not contain a participant ID.
The Social Discounting task short form contains one trial per distance level.  
This step converts the dataset from **wide format to long format**, which allows trial-level processing. After this step:

- `trial` contains the trial name (e.g., X1_SDshort_decision, X2_SDshort_decision)
- `max_rating` contains the participant’s response.
```{r SDS reshape_short}
data_wide_short2 <- data_wide_short[!is.na(data_wide_short$subnum), ]

longer_numeric_short <- pivot_longer(
  data_wide_short2,                         # pivot_longer keeps all other columns
  cols = matches("^X[1-7]_SDshort_decision$"),
  names_to = "trial",
  values_to = "max_rating"
)

```

```{r SDS split-trial-info}
longer_numeric_short$distance <- sub("_SDshort_decision", "", longer_numeric_short$trial)
```

### Remove Invalid/Missing Responses
This step:

- removes missing responses
- ensures `max_rating` values are numeric
```{r SDS filter-valid-trials}
filtered_data_short <- longer_numeric_short[!is.na(as.numeric(longer_numeric_short$max_rating)), ]
filtered_data_short <- subset(filtered_data_short, max_rating >= 0 & max_rating <= 10)

```

```{r SDS recode-distance}
trial_filtered_data_s <- filtered_data_short %>%
  dplyr::select(-any_of("X")) %>% 
  mutate(
    Distance = case_when(
      distance == "X1" ~ 1,
      distance == "X2" ~ 2,
      distance == "X3" ~ 5,
      distance == "X4" ~ 10,
      distance == "X5" ~ 20,
      distance == "X6" ~ 50,
      distance == "X7" ~ 100,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    )
  )

table(trial_filtered_data_s$max_rating)
```

## Analysis
This code uses the cleaned data to run the hyperbolic model, extract individual logk values and calculate individual AUC values

### Hyperbolic Model
The Social Discounting Task is typically analyzed using a hyperbolic discounting model, which estimates how generosity decreases as social distance increases.
The model estimates two parameters:

- v0: baseline generosity (at social distance = 0)
- logk: social discounting rate

Higher (less negative) logk values indicate steeper discounting across social distance.

#### Model 1: Base model (no predictors)
This model estimates the hyperbolic social discounting function without including any predictors. It is used to obtain **participant-level discounting parameters**, including logk, which reflects the rate of social discounting.

In most cases, researchers should run this model first and extract the **individual logk estimates** from it. These logk values can then be used in subsequent analyses (e.g., regression models) that include covariates or group variables.
Most users should run this model.

Starting values are chosen automatically with `fit_best_start()` (see Model Fitting Functions). `start_grid` lists the starting values to try for v0 and logk. Widen it if no starting values converge.

```{r SDS base-model}
# Starting values to try (short form: v0 between 0 and 10)
start_grid_s <- expand.grid(v0 = c(4, 7, 10), logk = c(-6, -4, -2, -1, 0))

hyp_fit_s <- function(st) nlme(as.numeric(max_rating) ~ v0 / (1 + exp(logk) * Distance),
                               fixed     = list(v0 ~ 1, logk ~ 1),
                               random    = v0 + logk ~ 1 | subnum,
                               start     = st,
                               data      = trial_filtered_data_s,
                               control   = ctl,
                               na.action = na.omit)

base_model_short <- fit_best_start(hyp_fit_s, start_grid_s)
summary(base_model_short)
attr(base_model_short, "start_search")   # every starting value tried and the result it reached
```

##### Comparison Models
We compare the hyperbolic model with an exponential and a linear model to confirm that the hyperbolic model fits best.

- **Exponential model:** like the hyperbolic model, it is parameterized with logk (k = exp(logk)), which keeps k positive. Its starting values are found with `fit_best_start()`. Note that the exponential logk is not on the same scale as the hyperbolic logk, so the two should not be compared directly.
- **Linear model:** this model is linear, so it is fit with `lme()`, which does not need starting values. `method = "ML"` is required so that its AICc can be compared with the `nlme` models.
```{r SDS alt models base}
# Exponential model
exp_fit_s <- function(st) nlme(as.numeric(max_rating) ~ v0 * exp(-exp(logk) * Distance),
                               fixed     = list(v0 ~ 1, logk ~ 1),
                               random    = v0 + logk ~ 1 | subnum,
                               start     = st,
                               data      = trial_filtered_data_s,
                               control   = ctl,
                               na.action = na.omit)

exponential_model_base <- fit_best_start(exp_fit_s, start_grid_s)
summary(exponential_model_base)

# Linear model
linear_model_base <- lme(as.numeric(max_rating) ~ Distance,
                         random    = ~ Distance | subnum,
                         data      = trial_filtered_data_s,
                         method    = "ML",
                         na.action = na.omit,
                         control   = lmeControl(opt = "optim"))
summary(linear_model_base)
```

##### Model Comparison (AICc Weights)
After fitting the hyperbolic, exponential, and linear models, we compare their relative fit using Akaike's Information Criterion corrected for sample size (AICc). AICc balances model fit and complexity: lower values indicate better-fitting models, with a penalty for additional parameters.

The `aic_table()` function (see Model Fitting Functions) returns one row per model, ranked from best to worst fit:

- K: number of estimated parameters
- LL: log-likelihood
- AICc
- Delta: ΔAICc, the difference between each model's AICc and the lowest AICc among the models
- Weight: AICc weight, the relative likelihood that each model is the best of the candidate models, calculated as
$$w_i = \frac{\exp(-\Delta_i / 2)}{\sum_j \exp(-\Delta_j / 2)}$$
- Cum_Weight: cumulative weight

We also calculate AIC weights directly from each model's AIC, without the small-sample correction:

- Extracts AIC for each model using `AIC()`
- Computes ΔAIC as the difference from the lowest AIC
- Calculates AIC weights using the same formula as above

With large samples (840 observations in the example data), AIC and AICc are nearly identical, so both tables lead to the same conclusions.

Interpretation: \ 

In most cases, the hyperbolic model will have the lowest AICc, so the exponential and linear models will have positive ΔAICc values. \ 
ΔAICc < 2 → substantial support (models are essentially equivalent) \ 
ΔAICc 4–7 → considerably less support \ 
ΔAICc > 10 → essentially no support (the model with the lower AICc fits better) \ 

AICc weights sum to 1 across the models. An AICc weight of 1 for the hyperbolic model means it is overwhelmingly the best-fitting model compared to the exponential and linear alternatives.
```{r SDS AIC_base}
models_base <- list(hyperbolic  = base_model_short,
                    exponential = exponential_model_base,
                    linear      = linear_model_base)

# AICc table (same values as aictab() in the AICcmodavg package)
AICc_table_base <- aic_table(models_base)
print(AICc_table_base)

# AIC weights (manual)
AICs_base <- sapply(models_base, AIC)
delta_base <- AICs_base - min(AICs_base)
weights_base <- exp(-0.5 * delta_base) / sum(exp(-0.5 * delta_base))


AIC_table_base <- data.frame(
  Model = names(AICs_base),
  AIC = as.numeric(AICs_base),
  Delta = delta_base,
  Weight = weights_base
)
print(AIC_table_base)
```
##### Extract logk
Below we extract individual logk values for each participant. 
In most cases, logk values should be extracted from the base model (Model 1). This ensures that individual discounting estimates are derived directly from task behavior and are not influenced by predictors included in the hyperbolic model. These participant-level logk values can then be used in subsequent analyses (e.g., regression models with covariates).

The code below combines the fixed effects and random effects to calculate participant-level logk estimates.

```{r SDS base logk}
cf_short <- coef(base_model_short)                     # fixed + random, one row per subnum
individual_logk_df_base_short <- data.frame(
  subnum    = type.convert(rownames(cf_short), as.is = TRUE),
  logk_base = cf_short$logk
)
head(individual_logk_df_base_short)
```

##### Check Against the True Values (Practice Data Only)
Same check for the short form, using `SDshortform_exampledata_trueparameters.csv`.

```{r SDS check true logk}
true_file_short <- file.path(path, sub("\\.csv$", "_trueparameters.csv", sd_short))

if (file.exists(true_file_short)) {
  true_short <- read.csv(true_file_short)

  check_short <- individual_logk_df_base_short %>%
    inner_join(true_short, by = "subnum")

  print(cor.test(check_short$logk, check_short$logk_base))
}
```

##### Extracting AUC \ 
Area under the curve (AUC) is computed using the trapezoidal method (trapz) across the observed social distance values (1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100). Because AUC is calculated over the actual range of x-values included in the task, the total span of the social distance axis is 100 − 1 = 99 units. The maximum possible AUC therefore corresponds to a participant consistently selecting the maximum forgone amount (10) across this range, yielding a value of 99 × 10 = 990. Observed AUC values were divided by 990 to yield a normalized index bounded between 0 and 1.
```{r SDS AUC_base}
trial_filtered_data2 <- dplyr::left_join(
  trial_filtered_data_s,
  individual_logk_df_base_short,
  by = "subnum"
)


AUC_short <- trial_filtered_data2 %>%
  group_by(subnum) %>%
  summarise(AUC = trapz(as.numeric(Distance), as.numeric(max_rating))/990, .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(
    trial_filtered_data2 %>%
      dplyr::distinct(subnum, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
      dplyr::select(-max_rating, -Distance, -any_of(c("distance", "trial"))),
    by = "subnum"
  )
```

#### Model 2: Model With Predictors (Optional)
You may want to examine how participant characteristics predict differences in the hyperbolic discounting function itself.
This model allows predictors (e.g., demographic variables, personality traits, or group membership) to explain variability in the discounting rate (logk).

This step is **optional** and is typically used only if the goal is to test predictors **directly within the hyperbolic model**, rather than analyzing extracted logk values in a separate model.

**Tips for using this model:**

Modify the predictors in the example to match the variables available in your dataset.

Set `n_extra` in `fit_best_start()` to the number of predictors in the model (5 in this example). The starting values for the predictor slopes are set to 0.
```{r SDS hyperbolic-predictor-example, eval = FALSE}

                                    fixed     = list(v0 ~ 1, logk ~ as.numeric(Male) + as.numeric(age) + as.numeric(income) +
                                as.numeric(FIT_sum) + as.numeric(Group_var)),
                                    random    = v0 + logk ~ 1 | subnum,
                                    start     = st,
                                    data      = trial_filtered_data_s,
                                    control   = ctl,
                                    na.action = na.omit)

predictor_model <- fit_best_start(pred_hyp_fit_s, start_grid_s, n_extra = 5)
summary(predictor_model)
attr(predictor_model, "start_search")
```


##### Comparison Models
We compare the hyperbolic model with an exponential and a linear model to confirm that the hyperbolic model fits best.

- **Exponential model:** like the hyperbolic model, it is parameterized with logk (k = exp(logk)), which keeps k positive. Its starting values are found with `fit_best_start()`. Note that the exponential logk is not on the same scale as the hyperbolic logk, so the two should not be compared directly.
- **Linear model:** this model is linear, so it is fit with `lme()`, which does not need starting values. `method = "ML"` is required so that its AICc can be compared with the `nlme` models. In `lme()`, a predictor's effect on the slope is written as an interaction with Distance (`Distance:predictor`), so the predictors affect the rate of decline, as in the hyperbolic and exponential models.
```{r SDS alt models pred, eval = FALSE}
# Exponential model
pred_exp_fit_s <- function(st) nlme(as.numeric(max_rating) ~ v0 * exp(-exp(logk) * Distance),
                                    fixed     = list(v0 ~ 1, logk ~ as.numeric(Male) + as.numeric(age) + as.numeric(income) +
                                                          as.numeric(FIT_sum) + as.numeric(Group_var)),
                                    random    = v0 + logk ~ 1 | subnum,
                                    start     = st,
                                    data      = trial_filtered_data_s,
                                    control   = ctl,
                                    na.action = na.omit)


exponential_model_pred <- fit_best_start(pred_exp_fit_s, start_grid_s, n_extra = 5)
summary(exponential_model_pred)

# Linear model
linear_model_pred <- lme(as.numeric(max_rating) ~ Distance +
                           Distance:(as.numeric(Male) + as.numeric(age) + as.numeric(income) +
          as.numeric(FIT_sum) + as.numeric(Group_var)),
                         random    = ~ Distance | subnum,
                         data      = trial_filtered_data_s,
                         method    = "ML",
                         na.action = na.omit,
                         control   = lmeControl(opt = "optim"))
summary(linear_model_pred)
```

##### Model Comparison (AICc Weights)
After fitting the hyperbolic, exponential, and linear models, we compare their relative fit using Akaike's Information Criterion corrected for sample size (AICc). AICc balances model fit and complexity: lower values indicate better-fitting models, with a penalty for additional parameters.

The `aic_table()` function (see Model Fitting Functions) returns one row per model, ranked from best to worst fit:

- K: number of estimated parameters
- LL: log-likelihood
- AICc
- Delta: ΔAICc, the difference between each model's AICc and the lowest AICc among the models
- Weight: AICc weight, the relative likelihood that each model is the best of the candidate models, calculated as
$$w_i = \frac{\exp(-\Delta_i / 2)}{\sum_j \exp(-\Delta_j / 2)}$$
- Cum_Weight: cumulative weight

We also calculate AIC weights directly from each model's AIC, without the small-sample correction:

- Extracts AIC for each model using `AIC()`
- Computes ΔAIC as the difference from the lowest AIC
- Calculates AIC weights using the same formula as above

With large samples (840 observations in the example data), AIC and AICc are nearly identical, so both tables lead to the same conclusions.

Interpretation: \ 

In most cases, the hyperbolic model will have the lowest AICc, so the exponential and linear models will have positive ΔAICc values. \ 
ΔAICc < 2 → substantial support (models are essentially equivalent) \ 
ΔAICc 4–7 → considerably less support \ 
ΔAICc > 10 → essentially no support (the model with the lower AICc fits better) \ 

AICc weights sum to 1 across the models. An AICc weight of 1 for the hyperbolic model means it is overwhelmingly the best-fitting model compared to the exponential and linear alternatives.
```{r SDS AIC_pred, eval = FALSE}
models_pred <- list(hyperbolic  = predictor_model,
                    exponential = exponential_model_pred,
                    linear      = linear_model_pred)

# AICc table (same values as aictab() in the AICcmodavg package)
AICc_table_pred <- aic_table(models_pred)
AICc_table_pred

# AIC weights (manual)
AICs_pred <- sapply(models_pred, AIC)
delta_pred <- AICs_pred - min(AICs_pred)
weights_pred <- exp(-0.5 * delta_pred) / sum(exp(-0.5 * delta_pred))
weights_pred

AIC_table_pred <- data.frame(
  Model = names(AICs_pred),
  AIC = as.numeric(AICs_pred),
  Delta = delta_pred,
  Weight = weights_pred
)
AIC_table_pred
```

##### Extracting logk values
 In the predictor model, each participant's logk depends on their predictor values. It is calculated as the participant-specific intercept (the fixed intercept plus that participant's random effect) plus each fixed slope multiplied by the participant's value on that predictor.
The code below:

- uses coef() to get each participant's model coefficients. The logk intercept already includes the participant's random effect.
- selects one row per participant from the data and puts the rows in the same order as the model output. Participants the model excluded (e.g., because of missing covariates) are dropped.
- creates a predictor matrix with each participant's covariate values. The predictors must match those in the hyperbolic model, in the same order.
- multiplies each participant's predictor values by the corresponding coefficients and sums them to get that participant's logk
- creates a dataset (individual_logk_df_pred) with one row per participant, containing the participant ID and estimated logk.

```{r SDS pred logk, eval = FALSE}
cf  <- coef(predictor_model)
pp  <- trial_filtered_data_s %>% distinct(subnum, .keep_all = TRUE)
pp  <- pp[match(type.convert(rownames(cf), as.is = TRUE), pp$subnum), ] #puts the rows in the same order as the participants in cf. also drops anyone that the model left out (ex: for missing a covariate)
X <- model.matrix(~ as.numeric(Male) + as.numeric(age) + as.numeric(income) +
                    as.numeric(FIT_sum) + as.numeric(Group_var),
                  data = pp) #builds a matrix

individual_logk_df_pred_short <- data.frame(
  subnum    = pp$subnum,
  logk_pred = rowSums(X * as.matrix(cf[, grep("^logk", names(cf))]))
)
```

##### Extracting AUC
```{r SDS pred AUC, eval = FALSE}
if (exists("AUC_short")) {
  AUC_short <- dplyr::left_join(
    AUC_short,
    individual_logk_df_pred_short,
    by = "subnum"
  )
} else {
  trial_filtered_data3 <- dplyr::left_join(
    trial_filtered_data_s,
    individual_logk_df_pred_short,
    by = "subnum"
  )
  
  AUC_short <- trial_filtered_data3 %>%
    group_by(subnum) %>%
    summarise(AUC = trapz(as.numeric(Distance), as.numeric(max_rating))/990, .groups = "drop") %>%
    left_join(
      trial_filtered_data3 %>%
        dplyr::distinct(subnum, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
        dplyr::select(-max_rating, -Distance, -any_of(c("distance","amount1","choice","trial"))),
      by = "subnum"
    )
}

```


### Graph of Social Discounting curve 

This code generates a plot of participants’ generosity across social distance, scaled as a proportion of the maximum possible amount (percentage). The workflow automatically adapts based on whether the dataset contains a grouping variable (Group):

- With "Group_var" present: The data are summarized separately for each group. The plot displays one line per group with shaded ribbons representing ±1 standard error of the mean. Groups are automatically labeled “Group1” and “Group2,” and color-coded for clarity.
- Without "Group_var": The data are summarized across all participants, producing a single hyperbolic curve with its standard error ribbon.

This approach ensures the graph works whether or not multiple groups are present, providing a clear visualization of social discounting behavior in your sample.

```{r SDS graph, echo = FALSE}
trial_filtered_data_s <- trial_filtered_data_s %>% mutate(percentage = as.numeric(max_rating) / 10)

if("Group_var" %in% colnames(trial_filtered_data_s)) {
  
  summary_data_s <- trial_filtered_data_s %>%
    group_by(Distance, Group_var) %>%
    summarise(payment = mean(percentage, na.rm = TRUE),
              ste = sd(percentage, na.rm = TRUE)/sqrt(n()),
              .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(Group = ifelse(Group_var == 1, "Group1", "Group2"))
  
  colors_mapping <- c("Group2" = "coral", "Group1" = "darkturquoise")
  
} else {
  
  summary_data_s <- trial_filtered_data_s %>%
    group_by(Distance) %>%
    summarise(payment = mean(percentage, na.rm = TRUE),
              ste = sd(percentage, na.rm = TRUE)/sqrt(n()),
              .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(Group = "All Participants")
  
  colors_mapping <- c("All Participants" = "darkturquoise")
}

# Plot curve
SD_APAplot_short <- ggplot(summary_data_s, aes(x = Distance, y = payment, color = Group, fill = Group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = payment - ste, ymax = payment + ste), alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(title = "Hyperbolic Social Discounting Curve",
       x = "Social Distance",
       y = "Proportion of $ Willing to Forgo") +
  scale_color_manual(values = colors_mapping) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colors_mapping) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_apa(base_size = 10, box = FALSE) +
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = "sans"),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 10, margin = margin(t = 10)),
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 10, margin = margin(r = 10)),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.line = element_line(colour = "black"),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 9)
  )

print(SD_APAplot_short)
```
### Graph of Both Forms Together

This code puts the long form (left) and short form (right) in one image:

- **Line:** the fitted hyperbolic curve, averaged across participants (each participant's curve uses their own v0 and logk from the base model)
- **Diamonds:** the actual mean proportion forgone at each social distance, with error bars showing ±1 standard error

If "Group_var" is present, each group gets its own line and diamonds. The image is also saved as a PNG in the folder set in `path`.

```{r SD graph both, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4}
# Average fitted curve: each participant's hyperbolic curve, averaged within group
make_curve <- function(model, data, max_amount) {
  cf  <- coef(model)
  ids <- data.frame(subnum = type.convert(rownames(cf), as.is = TRUE),
                    v0 = cf$v0, logk = cf$logk)  #grab each participant's own parameters
  if ("Group_var" %in% colnames(data)) {
    ids <- ids %>%
      left_join(data %>% distinct(subnum, Group_var), by = "subnum") %>%
      mutate(Group = ifelse(Group_var == 1, "Group1", "Group2"))
  } else {
    ids$Group <- "All Participants"
  }
  tidyr::expand_grid(ids, Distance = seq(1, 100, by = 0.5)) %>% #each person gets distances 1-100 by units of .5 to make the curve smooth, then uses this distance in the formula below to get the predicted value (in a proportion)
    mutate(fit = v0 / (1 + exp(logk) * Distance) / max_amount) %>%
    group_by(Group, Distance) %>%
    summarise(payment = mean(fit), .groups = "drop") #then you average across participants at each distance
}

form_levels <- c("Long Form", "Short Form")

curves_both <- bind_rows(
  make_curve(base_model_long,  trial_filtered_data,   80) %>% mutate(Form = "Long Form"),
  make_curve(base_model_short, trial_filtered_data_s, 10) %>% mutate(Form = "Short Form")
) %>% mutate(Form = factor(Form, levels = form_levels))

points_both <- bind_rows(
  summary_data_l %>% mutate(Form = "Long Form"),
  summary_data_s %>% mutate(Form = "Short Form")
) %>% mutate(Form = factor(Form, levels = form_levels))

SD_APAplot_both <- ggplot(points_both, aes(x = Distance, y = payment, color = Group)) +
  geom_line(data = curves_both, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = payment - ste, ymax = payment + ste), width = 2, color = "black") +
  geom_point(shape = 18, size = 3, color = "black") +                       # shape 18 = filled diamond
  facet_wrap(~ Form) +
  labs(title = "",
       x = "Social Distance",
       y = "Proportion of $ Willing to Forgo") +
  scale_color_manual(values = colors_mapping) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 10, 20, 50, 100)) +
  theme_apa(base_size = 12, box = FALSE) +
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = "sans"),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 26, margin = margin(t = 10)),
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 26, margin = margin(r = 10)),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 26),
    axis.line = element_line(colour = "black"),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 26, face = "bold"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 20),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 20)
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = if (n_distinct(points_both$Group) > 1) "right" else "none")   # no legend when there is only one group
print(SD_APAplot_both)

ggsave(file.path(path, "SD_curves_long_and_short.png"), SD_APAplot_both,
       width = 8, height = 4, dpi = 500)
```
